7: A marvellous and comic tale, by J.A.
9: Children, come and listen to me; I shall tell you here how Mr Prikkebeen fared,
10: who so loved to catch butterflies, yet whose sister Urso wished he would give up the chase.
11: Hear how, at his wits' end, he flees from sister Urso.
12: How a whale swallows him up, skin and hair and all.
13: And how at last the poor wretch must shrink upon the roasting-spit.
14: All that befell him you shall hear in this song.
15: And though it sometimes sounds a little strange, what is printed here is true.
18: How Mr Prikkebeen delights in catching butterflies.
19: Early in the morning Prikkebeen trudges busily through thick and thin.
20: Catching butterflies in his net is his greatest delight.
21: And if they forbade him that, he would surely kneel himself to death.
22: Has he after long chase caught one?
23: Oh, how sweetly then does Prikkebeen laugh!
24: He pins the little creature on his hat.
25: And no king's golden crown seems half so fair in his eyes.
26: When at last he comes home weary in the evening with his treasure, all is neatly arranged and pinned fast in little boxes.
27: Rich as Croesus in appearance, Prikkebeen was known as a poor man.
28: Even before he goes to sleep, standing in his shirt as good as bare,
29: he takes up such a little beast and examines it from top to toe.
30: As shown here, he grins with pleasure.
31: And even at night in bed, with his nightcap on his head,
32: he dreams of a magic land where butterflies sit on the walls and beetles fly everywhere without number.
33: Early, before day and dew, he stands ready again beside his bed, humming:
34: I wonder what I shall catch today.
36: I advise you, man, do pull your trousers on first.
38: How Mr Prikkebeen writes his sister a farewell letter.
39: Alas, it was a pity that Prikkebeen had an angry sister who daily scolded him so that he would not stay at home with her.
40: Until at last he set down on paper this short note.
41: Dear sister Ursula, I am going to America.
42: That is truly the land of butterflies.
43: I write you this in my own hand and remain, as before, your faithful Prikkebeen.
47: She snatches the letter at once; the poor simpleton Prikkebeen stands trembling with fright.
48: Urso flushes red as blood, seizes his net and shrieks furiously:
51: You wanted to go away and leave me?
52: Trembling, frightened, pale as a sheet, our Prikkebeen crawls into a corner.
53: Urso stands square before him, looks at him with angry eyes,
54: taps him on his long nose and says: Now tell me honestly—do you want to travel, dear brother?
57: It does not taste good to him.
58: Full of regret and grief he sits there and speaks not a word.
59: Urso, hearing him sigh, says at last: Come, speak a little.
60: Do not be so sad, my treasure.
61: Come, to please you I shall play a little on the piano
62: and with her shrill voice she sings a very pretty song for him.
63: But he listens, humming, and thinks: You can go to the moon.
64: At last he can bear it no longer.
65: Let me go, sister, he cries aloud.
66: But she shouts: That you shall not.
67: You will stay quietly here, man.
68: Whereupon she slaps the table so that everything turns upside down.
69: Now Prikkebeen has waited until the dead of night.
70: And then he steals like a mouse on tiptoe out of the house.
72: If it can be, I hope never to see you again.
74: How Mr Prikkebeen sets out on his journey and leaves Europe by ship.
75: And when he now went travelling, what was the first thing he caught?
76: In his net a grenadier, on his hat a woman.
77: Uproar and abuse were not lacking.
78: Everyone thought him mad, yet far into the night he kept on with his chase.
79: Until a bat, shy of the light, came flying into his face.
80: That ended the sport, and he sought a lodging.
81: At last, after a day or two, he came to the seashore, where a ship lay ready to sail.
82: At that joyful sight Mr Prikkebeen rejoiced aloud and straightway made up his mind.
83: In a little boat he rows away towards the great ship and goes aboard.
84: Cheerfully he waves cap and hat.
87: Complain now to sister Ursula and go to America.
88: Ah, scarcely has he come aboard
89: when who catches him by the coat-tails?
90: His dear little sister Ursula had followed him, saw how he went aboard, and now grabs him by his coat.
91: She weeps and wails until he has promised to give up his foolish butterfly-catching for life.
92: Prikkebeen strolls mute and glum with her about the ship.
93: Urso plays blindman's buff with dear brother for his pleasure; the simpleton gropes about
94: until at last, as his prize, he clasped Ursula in his arms.
96: Quickly he pulls the cloth over her eyes and then slips softly from the cabin down the stairs.
97: Ursula is left alone and seeks Prikkebeen in vain.
98: On deck he stands sighing ah and oh,
99: because he may never again go butterfly-hunting.
